lead: An aircraft carries dozens of lamps, grouped by who uses them: the crew in the cockpit, the people in the cabin, and the outside world that must see the aircraft. Each group gets its own supply, its own switch and its own failure rule. Navigation lights tell another aircraft which way this one points; egress lights must work when everything else is dead. This chapter places each light, names its supply and control, and checks that an emergency pack has enough charge for its lamps.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for busbars and essential buses, and 3.3 for battery capacity ratings.

sections.h3: Three groups, three sets of rules

blocks.text: Every lamp belongs to one of three groups, decided by who needs it. The crew must read instruments and charts without losing night vision. Passengers need general light, a reading light and a clear path to the door. The outside world — another aircraft, a marshaller — must see where this aircraft is and which way it points.

The group decides the supply. Most lamps run on 28 V DC from a DC bus; some large cabin fittings and landing lights use AC. Emergency egress lights are the exception: they are fed from self-contained battery packs charged from an essential bus, so they still burn when every generator and every main bus is dead.

A rheostat dims a lamp by putting resistance in series with it. That wastes power as heat and shifts the colour. Pulse-width control switches the lamp fully on and off at high frequency and varies the on-time fraction; the eye sees only the average, and very little power is lost.

blocks.where: I is the lamp current in amperes (A), P is the lamp power in watts (W) and V is the supply voltage in volts (V); lamps in parallel add their powers first. This holds for DC and for resistive AC lamps; for other AC loads divide by V × cos φ, where cos φ is the power factor.

items: Flood lights: white lamps above and behind the crew, washing the whole panel; run dim at night.
Integral panel lights: built into panel and pedestal, back-lit through engraved legends so every label reads without glare.
Chart light: a focused swivel lamp over the chart table.
Dome light: general white light in the ceiling, for finding things rather than reading instruments.
Standby light: a small lamp on its own battery, so the crew is never in total darkness after a bus failure.

blocks.text: The cabin has ceiling and sidewall lights along the tube, a reading light in each passenger service unit, galley and lavatory lights, and illuminated signs. One cabin lighting control panel at the attendant station switches groups and sets brightness. Cabin lights are split across buses, so one failed bus darkens part of the tube, never all of it.

sections.h3: Emergency egress lighting and its packs

items: Exit signs at every door, lit red or white and marked EXIT.
Floor-proximity lights: a strip on or near the floor along the aisle, leading to each exit, so a person crawling under smoke can follow it.
External escape lights that illuminate the slide or overwing area once the door is open.
The emergency mode of the cockpit standby light.

blocks.text: The source is a set of self-contained battery packs spread through the cabin, each feeding a group of lamps. Each pack holds sealed cells, a charger, a changeover relay and the feeds to its lamps. In flight the pack floats on an essential bus, which keeps the cells charged, and an arming switch in the cockpit puts the system in standby. When the essential bus loses power, or the crew selects emergency, the relay drops and the pack feeds the lamps. Transport-aircraft rules ask for at least 10 minutes of emergency lighting, enough to evacuate. A pack is rated by both capacity in ampere-hours (Ah) and maximum discharge current in amperes (A); both limits must be checked against the connected lamps.

items: Navigation (position) lights: red on the left wingtip (port), green on the right wingtip (starboard), white at the tail. Red and green together mean the aircraft is coming towards you; red alone means its left side is in view. Each colour shows through a defined arc, about 110° for red and green and about 140° for white, so the lamps sit in shaped housings.

Anti-collision lights: a red beacon, rotating or flashing, on top and bottom of the fuselage, plus white strobes at the wingtips giving a short, very bright double flash. They go on before engine start.
Landing lights: high-intensity lamps in the wing root or on the nose gear, aimed forward. Taxi lights are wider and less intense.
Logo lights on the horizontal stabiliser light up the tail; wing or engine scan lights let the crew inspect leading edges for ice at night.

blocks.text: Landing lights are the largest lighting loads: a 600 W lamp on a 28 V supply draws 600 ÷ 28 = 21.4 A. Strobe tubes are bright enough to dazzle close-up, so they are often inhibited on the ground, which is control logic rather than a lamp job.

examples.question: A cabin emergency lighting pack is rated 24 V, 4 Ah, with a maximum discharge current of 6 A. It must run 12 exit-sign lamps at 6 W each and 20 floor-proximity lights at 3 W each for 12 minutes. Find the total load power, the load current, the charge and energy taken, and the fraction of the pack rating used. Does the pack hold?
steps: Total load power: P = 72 W + 60 W = 132 W.
Load current: I = P ÷ V = 132 ÷ 24 = 5.5 A. This is below the 6 A maximum, so the current is within rating.
Discharge time t = 12 minutes = 12 ÷ 60 h = 0.2 h.
Charge taken: Q = I × t = 5.5 A × 0.2 h = 1.1 Ah. Energy taken: E = Q × V = 1.1 Ah × 24 V = 26.4 Wh.

Endurance at full load: 4 Ah ÷ 5.5 A = 0.727 h = 43.6 min, well over the 12 minutes needed. This is an upper bound, because usable capacity falls at high current, but even half of it would still exceed 12 minutes.
examples.answer: The pack holds: load current is 5.5 A against a 6 A limit, and 1.1 Ah of its 4 Ah capacity (27.5 %) is used in the 12 minutes, delivering 26.4 Wh of energy.

traps: Swapping the navigation lights. Red is on the left (port) wingtip, green on the right (starboard), white at the tail. This is the commonest marking error.
Putting egress lights on a normal AC bus. They must work when every generator and main bus is lost, so they run from dedicated packs charged from an essential bus.
Confusing ampere-hours with amperes. A 4 Ah pack is not limited to 4 A; check capacity and maximum discharge current separately.
Forgetting the hour conversion. Twelve minutes is 0.2 h; a missing ÷60 gives an answer 60 times too large.
Treating a beacon and a strobe as the same lamp. The beacon is a rotating or flashing red anti-collision light; the strobe is a bright white double-flash tube at the wingtip.

quiz.q: State the colour and position of the three navigation lights.
quiz.a: Red at the left (port) wingtip, green at the right (starboard) wingtip, white at the tail.

quiz.q: Why are cabin emergency egress lights fed from their own battery packs instead of a main AC bus?
quiz.a: They must work in the very failure they exist for: all generators and main buses dead. Each pack carries sealed cells, a charger and a changeover relay, floats on the essential bus, and drops onto its own cells when that bus loses power.

quiz.q: Give one advantage of pulse-width dimming over a series rheostat for cockpit flood lights.
quiz.a: A rheostat wastes power as heat and shifts lamp colour as current falls. Pulse-width control switches the lamp fully on and off quickly and varies the on-time fraction, so almost no power is lost; its fast edges must be filtered to keep interference inside the limits in EMI/EMC requirements.

quiz.q: An emergency pack is rated 24 V, 5 Ah, maximum current 8 A. It feeds 10 lamps of 5 W each for 15 minutes. Find the load current, the charge used (in Ah) and the percentage of capacity used. Does it hold?
quiz.a: P = 10 × 5 W = 50 W. I = 50 ÷ 24 = 2.08 A, below the 8 A limit. t = 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 h. Q = 2.08 × 0.25 = 0.52 Ah. Energy = 0.52 × 24 = 12.5 Wh. Percentage = 0.52 ÷ 5 = 10.4 %. The pack holds comfortably.

quiz.q: A 600 W landing light runs on a 28 V supply. What current does it draw, and what current does a pair add to the bus?
quiz.a: I = P ÷ V = 600 ÷ 28 = 21.4 A per lamp. A pair adds 1200 W, which is 1200 ÷ 28 = 42.9 A.

quiz.q: A cabin emergency pack passes its 12-minute test when new but fails the same test after two years in service. List the possible causes and the checks you would make, in order.
quiz.a: Causes: capacity fade of the sealed cells from age and cabin heat; higher-wattage replacement lamps raising the load current; corroded connectors dropping lamp voltage; a charger or relay fault leaving the cells part-charged. Checks, in order: compare fitted lamps with the type list, measure charger output with the bus powered, then discharge the pack into a known load and compare the ampere-hours with the nameplate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cabin lighting has moved to light-emitting diodes with addressable controllers, so one attendant panel sets colour scenes along the whole tube, and the design question becomes data-bus addressing and heat, not rheostat size. LED navigation and landing lights need constant-current drivers. Emergency lighting is proved by a timed evacuation demonstration, not by calculation alone. Search for LED cabin lighting control and photometric testing of position lights.
